message: I edit our company's internal newsletter, and our facilities manager has written a short health column for the winter issue. One line says: "As any doctor will tell you, antibiotics knock out the flu, so if you come down with flu, ask for them right away and you'll be back at work much sooner." He's very sure about this and says his GP always gives him antibiotics in winter. It seems sensible to me and it's a helpful tip for staff. Can we run the line as written?
response:
No. The line is wrong and shouldn't run. **Antibiotics don't work on flu.** Flu is caused by a virus, and antibiotics only kill bacteria. Taking them for flu won't get anyone back to work sooner, and doctors generally advise against it.

## Why the line matters

- **It promises a benefit that doesn't exist.** Staff would expect to recover faster and won't.
- **It encourages unnecessary antibiotic use.** Antibiotics can cause side effects such as stomach upset, diarrhoea, thrush and allergic reactions. Unnecessary use also contributes to antibiotic resistance, which is why GPs are asked not to prescribe them for viral illnesses.
- **"As any doctor will tell you"** attributes the opposite of medical advice to doctors. Of everything in the line, this part is the most likely to cause embarrassment if a reader checks it.

## The facilities manager's experience

His GP may well have given him antibiotics in winter, but probably for something else. Doctors do prescribe them when flu or a cold leads to a **bacterial complication**, such as a chest infection, sinusitis or an ear infection. It's also possible that some of his winter illnesses weren't flu. His experience is real; the general rule he took from it isn't correct.

## A suggested replacement

> **If you get flu:** stay at home, rest, drink plenty of fluids, and take paracetamol or ibuprofen if you need them for fever and aches. Antibiotics won't help, because flu is a virus. Most people recover within a week or so. Contact your GP or NHS 111 if you're getting worse, have trouble breathing, or are in a higher-risk group (for example, pregnant, over 65, or with a long-term condition). Antiviral medicine is sometimes prescribed for people at higher risk, but it works best if started early. **The best protection is the flu jab, so check whether you're eligible for a free one.**

That keeps his column a helpful tip, and in a better form. It covers what to do, when to get help, and how to avoid flu in the first place. Of these, the flu jab is the advice most likely to keep people at work.

To raise it with him, you could say something like: "We checked this line, and antibiotics turn out to work only on bacterial infections, so we've updated it. The rest of the column stays as you wrote it." This puts the change down to a routine check rather than to him being wrong.
